title: A Pelter's Reckoning
author: a pelter who went further down than he meant to
body:
# Skins

*Cut into the hide side, small.*

---

Spring. Four skins at the mouth. Good grey-gold, the Tamwick tanners give two marks the skin.

Midsummer. Nine skins in the first chamber. They lie up in fours and they do not run from a lamp. Kester says they are waiting for something.

After the Long Table. Kester went down to the lake chamber for the big dog-wolf. He came back up without his knife and would not say. He says there is a white cord running down the wall all the way and something at the bottom of it keeps it tight.

They are not wolves at the bottom. I mean they are, but they are the Hound's.

*Last, in a worse hand:* The Hounders were right. Scour the figure. Somebody scour the figure.

title: The Drovers' Last Tally
author: the eastern drovers, on the board inside the pound gate
body:
# Counted In

*Notches, and under them words burned in with a hot nail.*

---

Brow ewes, Rookdown mark: nine score and four. Counted in at dusk.

Bram Down wethers: three score. Counted in.

Southgate's heifers: eleven. Counted in. Hesta says pay her in news at the other end.

---

*Burned deeper:* The gate is shut. Word came up from the Southgate Stone at dark. The Briar has shut its gate and the thorn is across it and nobody is to go east. We will take them home in the morning.

*There is no line for the morning. Nobody counted them out. The last flock the pound held is still, on this board, in it.*

title: Hedda's Kiln-Book
author: Hedda Limeburner of Cressbourne
body:
# Burns

*A careful hand. Figures down the side.*

---

**Naming Day.** Both kilns charged. Chalk from the top bench, flint picked out by Col. Burned three days. Drew forty bushel quick.

**After.** Merrowby for whitewash, twelve bushel. Cress Mill for the leat walls, four. Tamwick orchards to sweeten the ground, ten.

**For the south.** Ashway, as every spring: fourteen bushel to lime the headland on the grey side. Rab says it is superstition and pays for it every year and his furrow has never gone grey. I say lime is lime and the grey is the grey and I do not know what one does to the other. I only know the Ashways have limed that headland since my grandmother's time, and the grey has kept a furrow off.

**Midsummer.** The south cart is loaded. Col will not take it past the Hare and Hurdle. He says the bristlebacks are down the cut every dusk and a boy on a cart is a thing a boar looks at. He is not wrong. He is also not taking it.

title: The Places at the Long Table
author: Oswen Bellsey, Table-Warden of the Brow
body:
# The Brow Long Table: the places

*Written fresh every harvest and read aloud before the first loaf is cut.*

---

At the head, Rookdown: the Rookwrights, the Rookwells, the Southcotes (who come back for this and nothing else), the Wax house, the miller's.

Down the middle, the farms: Brow End, Southgate, the Hatchmoors, Coldharbour, Ashway.

At the Bramcombe end: the Droves, the shepherds' houses, and whoever the flocks brought down.

## At the foot

The bells of lines that have ended, buried, with the handles up so they can be rung for on the day:

The Cadwell bell. The Pennock bell. The Tiler bell. The Hurdwell bell, last buried, Y.T. 1039, when old Anse Hurdwell died with nobody after him.

*A note pinned to the roll:* The Hurdwell hole is empty. I rang for them anyway. I rang the air where the bell was. The table heard it. OB.

title: Enid Drove's Evening Count
author: Enid Drove, head shepherd of Bramcombe
body:
# Count

*Two columns on a slate. The first headed FIRST, the second AGAIN.*

---

FIRST: seven score and six.  AGAIN: seven score and seven.

FIRST: seven score and six.  AGAIN: seven score and seven.

FIRST: seven score and five (the lame one to Bramcombe).  AGAIN: seven score and six.

---

*Underneath, pressed hard:* There is always one more on the second count. It is never the same ewe. I have walked the fold with the lantern and looked at every face, and every face is mine, and there is one more. She does not bleat. She stands at the hurdle on the Hush side and looks at the wheelhouse.

I have not told Bramcombe. They would want me down. I have had this down forty summers and I am not coming off it for a ewe.

title: The Southcote Plough-Book
author: the Southcotes of the Brow, and after them somebody else
body:
# The Terraces

*A farm's book: every terrace named, and what was sown on it, and who turned it, going back three hundred years in a dozen hands.*

---

**Top Step.** Barley. Turned by Oswy Southcote. Buried at the top hedge with his spade, Y.T. 812.

**Long Step.** Beans. Turned by Madlin Southcote and her sister. Buried at the long hedge with the sickle between them, Y.T. 870.

**Hush Step.** Fallow. Nobody likes to turn it.

---

*The last pages are in a different ink, and the hand is square and slow, as if each letter were a furrow:*

Top Step. Turned. Long Step. Turned. Hush Step. Turned, to the grey. The grey is soft to turn. We are behind. The family has gone to Rookdown and left the book and we are behind, and every morning the grey has come up a little, and every night we turn it back.

title: This Season's Tally at Briarfoot
author: the Wardens keeping Briarfoot Watch
body:
# Briarfoot: what was seen

*Two hands, turn and turn about, and one line in a third.*

---

First week. Gate shut. Thorn across it as ever. No lights. The grey a stride and a half off the Southgate Stone. OF.

Second week. A thorn fallen on the Vale side, grey, did not rot. Left it. JC.

Third week. Woodfolk on the far side of the thorn at dusk, three, looking at the tower. Waved. They did not. OF.

Fourth week. The grey a stride off the Stone. JC.

*In a third hand, low on the board, where a person would chalk if they were kneeling:* It is not coming to the Stone. It is coming to the tower. Ask who is on the terraces at midnight.

*Under that, in the first hand:* Neither of us wrote that. OF. *And the second:* I know. JC.

title: Scions and Stocks
author: Russet Graft, who keeps the Mother Pippin for Tamwick
body:
# Where the Mother's children went

*Every scion cut from the Mother Pippin, and where it was grafted, and whether it took.*

---

Tamwick, the long orchard: forty scions, all took. They always take in Tamwick.

Ridgeway, the Vale side of the house: six, all took. The Wold side: six, none took. Wil says the Wold side keeps its own trees. He is right.

Hazel Bottom: four, three took.

Brow End: two, both took and bear red, which the Mother's children never do. Aud says it is the byre door.

---

No farm south of the Hare and Hurdle has ever had an apple tree. I have offered scions to every one of them every winter for twenty years. They say, kindly, that apples are Tamwick's, and they are frightened of something they will not name, and I think it is this: a tree takes a lifetime to bear, and they are not sure they will be there.

title: The Scouring Song
author: the Hounders, as it is sung round the figure
body:
# The Scouring Song

*Sung walking, one verse to each part of the Hound, in this order and no other.*

---

**The nose.** White nose, keep to the ground; / there is nothing to follow, nothing is found.

**The ear.** White ear, lie flat and be still; / the wind on the down is the wind on the hill.

**The back.** White back, long as a drove; / lie in the chalk that the Hounders wove.

**The tail.** White tail, curl and stay curled; / sleep is the kindest thing in the world.

**The eye.** *(Sung last, standing in it.)* White eye, shut. / White eye, shut. / White eye, shut.

---

*Pencilled under it:* We sing the eye three times because it is the part that opens. Aldous sang it four times, the last summer, to be sure. It was not enough.

title: The Listener's Book, This Year
author: Linnet Crale, Listener of the Brow for the Wardens
body:
# Heard on the Brow

*Each verse written down as it was heard, with the night, the wind and where the Listener stood.*

---

**New moon, no wind, at the shieling door.**
*Four voices. Low.* We kept the note, we kept the note, / and the note kept us, and we were not afraid.

**Half moon, a little east, at the shieling door.**
*Two voices, a child's and an old man's.* Say it at the door and say it at the well, / say it at the table, and the lark will tell.

---

*Three pages with headings and nothing under them:*

**At the last of the Hush Steps.**
**Between the Hushwatch stones.**
**Among the cliff graves.**

*And under the last:* The verses are loudest in these three places and I cannot go to them at night any more. My knees. My nerve. Mostly my nerve. LC.

title: Bel Axtree's List
author: Bel Axtree, widow of Tom Axtree, carter
body:
# The Wheels

*From the end nearest the fort.*

---

1. Cob Ferrier of Tamwick. Would not pay. Found in the ditch by his cart.
2. The Pennock boy. His father paid; the boy said he would not, on the way back. Found by the Hare Stone.
3. Tom Axtree, my Tom. Would not pay. Said a mark a wheel was a tax and a tax was the Tallymen's business, not a carter's. I found him.
4. Ide Wheeler. Would not pay. Found.
5. A carter nobody knew, from the east, with a Woodfolk wheel. Found.

---

The captain writes everybody down. He wrote Tom down. It is in his book, in the other ink, what was done and who did it and on which day. I want it out of his book. I do not know yet whether I want to read it.

title: The Road Crew's Pay-Book
author: the paymaster of the Vale road crew, Y.T. 0
body:
# Pay

*Columns: the name, the days worked, the marks paid.*

---

Abel Larkbourne, ganger. Ninety days. Paid.
Hob Larkbourne. Ninety days. Paid.
Wat Stonecart. Eighty days. Paid.
Cadell Brook. Ninety days. Paid.
*(and forty names more, all paid)*

---

*At the foot of the last page, the paymaster's own words:*

The bell is down and the roads are laid and there is no more work. Every man above is paid in full to this day and owes nothing and is owed nothing. Let that be written somewhere, since the Wardens say a crew with no road is nobody's neighbour, and will not write them on their Roll.

They are written here. This is a book too.

title: The Kennel Book
author: Garrick Coupler, kennel-master to the Wardens' Rest
body:
# The Pack

*Nine couple. Each hound by name and dam.*

---

Bellmouth, out of Tollie. Lead hound. Will not give tongue on a false line.
Ruby and Rake, out of Bellmouth. Ruby is the nose, Rake is the voice.
Old Sorrow, out of nobody knows. Came to the kennel gate as a pup in the Quiet Villages years and was let in.
*(and fourteen more, with their dams)*

---

*The last page:*

Midnight. Not a sound out of any of them, which is the thing I cannot get past: eighteen hounds over a wall and not one gave tongue. Old Sorrow went first. The rest went after her the way they go after Bellmouth on a true line.

West. Toward the Holt. The wolves were calling from the Holt the three nights before, and I thought it was only wolves.

I have chained the gate from outside. If they come back they will find it shut, and they will know it was them that left.

title: The Board Not Yet Struck
author: the Wardens' sign-painter, not yet finished
body:
# A name-board

*White letters on a black board, the Wardens' hand.*

---

RYN LARKBOURNE

*No stroke through it. On the back, in chalk, in a hand that is used to chalking numbers on walls:*

They have painted it and they have not struck it. That is the Wardens asking. They have never asked before.

If I come in off the road, the stroke is never painted and the board comes down. If I do not, it is struck, and it hangs here with Grandad's and all the others till the weather has it.

I came up to read it at night so the lads would not see me read it. I have read it eleven nights. I cannot read it twelve.

title: The Pit-Reckoning
author: the farms of Hound Down, every Long Table
body:
# The kept pit

*Cut on a stick, one notch a farm a year. The farms' marks are burned in at the top.*

---

Hurdlegate, Hatchmoor, Coldharbour, Ashway, the Hare and Hurdle, the Hounders: one notch each, every Long Table since the Ash Winter.

---

*A strip of paper wound round the stick, in a Warden's hand:*

The kept pit is not to be opened until a winter the Wardens call. The ash came in 866 and the down lived on what was in the chalk. It will not come the same way twice. It may come some other way. Keep the pit.

*Under it, in pencil, recent:* Lid moved. Three sacks short. Boar tracks round the pit, and a man's, and the man's go down and do not come up.

title: What Rookdown Told the Bees
author: Tibby Wax, bee-keeper of Rookdown
body:
# Told

*A line for each telling, and who told it.*

---

The Rookwright girl is to be married at harvest. Told by her mother.

Old Anse Hurdwell has died and his line with him. Told by Oswen Bellsey, who rang for him.

The beacon was lit on the Brow. Told by me, because nobody else would come up.

The beacon was lit again. Told by me.

A stranger slept in the Rookwells' barn and left before light. Told by Maud Rookwell, who walked up from the Grey End to do it.

---

*Not yet told:* the grey on the green has reached the well. I have sat on the bench with it three evenings. I cannot say it to them. If a stranger said it, they would take it better. They like to be told by somebody who means it and does not have to live with it.

title: The Ash Watch Log
author: the keepers of Ash Watch, nine days each
body:
# Ash Watch

*Each keeper nine days. Each keeper a line a day.*

---

Day one. The glass bed quiet. Pilgrims going down, two. Coming back, none.

Day four. A light out on the ash where no light should be. Watched it an hour. It went south, slowly, the way a person walks who is not tired.

Day nine. Handing over. Nothing to report but the light. I have looked at the ash nine days and I would like to look at something else now. — CF

---

*The next keeper, day one:* I have been told why it is nine days. I did not believe it. I have been here since dawn and I believe it.

title: Hound Watch: the Keeper's Log
author: Morwen Dagley, keeper of Hound Watch
body:
# Hound Watch

*A line a day, and a mark for the bell: rung or not rung.*

---

Clear. The Choir's heads plain as teeth. Not rung.

Mist. Could not see the Choir. Could see the Stair. Somebody on the piers. Not rung, because I could not say who.

Clear. The Choir. The Stair. The Vale, all of it, as far as the Mere, and every house in it I know somebody in. Not rung.

---

*In the margin, larger:* They build the watch here because you can see everything. Nobody says what it is like to see everything every day. The Wardens send us wine. I know why.

*And below:* The wolves are coming up out of the south flank in fours. I can see them from the crown. They do not look up at the tower. They look at the Hound.

title: The Beacon-Keeper's Reckoning
author: Edwy Marl, keeper of the Brow Beacon
body:
# Burned

*Copied from the old book into the new, so they are all in one place.*

---

Y.T. 951. Burned. Something on the Hush cliffs. Rookdown shut its doors. Nothing came.
Y.T. 981. Burned eleven nights, the nights the Toll hummed. Gosford went quiet on the tenth.
Y.T. 1003. Burned. A ship on the Hush, which cannot be.
Y.T. 1027. Burned. By a keeper who was ill. Stood down in the morning.

**Y.T. 1043, spring.** Burned. The Toll hummed.
**Y.T. 1043, spring.** Burned again. Singing on the Brow, loud enough to hear from here over the wind.

---

Wood in the stack: enough for nine nights. I have asked Rookdown for more. They have sent more. They did not ask why.

title: A Shepherd's Knot at the Holt
author: a Fallowfold shepherd, a long time ago
body:
# The knot, read

*A Fallowfold counting-cord: each knot a word, as the West Downs shepherds tie them. Read from the loop end.*

---

Wall. High. Wolves. No.

Marsh. Rising. Wolves. Come.

Fold. Leave. Flock. Home.

Fold. Ours. Always.

---

*The last knot is tied in a different cord, newer, black with grease: a hound's knot, the kind the Wardens' kennel uses on a leash.* Somebody has been here since, and tied on to the shepherds' cord the one word a kennel-master ties when a hound is lost: *called.*

title: A Child's Slate
author: a child of Rookdown
body:
# A slate

*Big letters, the S backwards.*

---

I SAID THE NAME. MAM SAID SAY ONE NAME AND GO HOME.

I SAID ISSOLT LARKSTEAD.

NOBODY KNOWS WHO THAT IS. MAM SAID WHERE DID YOU GET THAT. I SAID THE STONES SAID IT FIRST.

*Under it, in a grown hand, smaller:* The Wardens have been told. The Listener on the Brow has been told. Nobody is to scold her. She said it right.

title: Arrows That Do Not Miss
author: Hale Thornsby of the Woodfolk
body:
# The grey thorn

*Burned along the stick in small letters, Woodfolk-fashion.*

---

Cut at the Grey End: a thorn a day, no more, and never from the living side.

The grey thorn makes a shaft that does not miss. That is true. What the Vale does not ask is what it does not miss. It goes where it is meant to go, and it is not always meant by the one who looses it.

The Wold sends me here because I am the only fletcher who will say that out loud and still cut it.

title: The Fire-Keepers' Rota
author: the households of Rookdown
body:
# Who keeps the fire

*A painted board. Each night of the month a house.*

---

The Rookwrights. The Rookwells. The Wax house. The mill. Brow End. The Southcotes (painted out). The Southcotes (painted in again, smaller, by somebody who did not ask).

---

*Chalked across the top:* Nobody knows who it was lit for. We keep it because it has always been kept, and because the night it goes out, whoever it was lit for will look up the cliff and see nothing, and we would rather not be the house that did that.

title: The Lintel at Lamb's Bottom
author: the shepherd who built the hut
body:
# Under the lintel

*Cut into the chalk underside, shallow.*

---

BUILT BY COLE PENNOCK FOR HIS FLOCK AND HIS DOG. THE DOG IS CALLED WAIT.

*And later, deeper, the letters hurried:*

GOING SOUTH. THE SINGING SAYS COME. WAIT STAYS. KEEP THE HUT, WAIT.

*There are wolf-scratches all round the lintel's edge, very old, and none across the words.*

title: The Sheepwash Tally
author: the Fallowfold shepherds
body:
# Washed

*A notch a flock, three hundred years of them, the old notches worn to dimples.*

---

*The note tied to it, recent:*

The spring went up the hill the year Wynstead's meadows drowned. We carry buckets after it. We wash the flocks in buckets and put the notch on this board as if they went through the pool.

The Wardens say that is how a place stays a place: you keep doing the thing it was for, even when you have to carry the water. My back says otherwise. My back does not get a vote.

title: The Hayward's Pound-Book
author: Merrowby's hayward
body:
# Penned

*The beast, whose, and the penny.*

---

A sow, the Larkfields'. Penny paid.
Two ewes, Wynstead mark. Penny paid.
A goat, nobody's. Kept a week. Given to Ashwell for the well-warden's children.
A red heifer, Brow End mark, a long way from home. Penny paid by Aud, who walked from the Brow and did not complain and complained all the way back.

---

*Last line:* A ewe with no mark at all and grey to the skin. Penned at dusk. Gone at dawn with the gate still shut and the bell not rung. No penny. I have not written whose.

title: A Carter's Rain-Count
author: a Merrowby carter
body:
# Rings

*A crossing a line: rang once, rang twice, and the weather after.*

---

Once. Fair.
Once. Fair.
Twice. Rain by noon. As they say.
Twice. Rain by noon.
Three times. Never heard of three times. Clear as glass all day, and the Toll hummed that night up over Merrowby.

---

*Under it:* Carters say twice means rain. Nobody has a saying for three. I have made one: three times, go home.

title: Scratchings in the Spray Caves
author: somebody who sheltered behind the falls
body:
# Behind the water

*Scratched small, the lines crooked.*

---

Went in behind the falls to get out of the rain. Wolves in the back of the cave, three, asleep. Did not wake them.

The water is so loud in there you cannot hear yourself, and I thought: this is the one place in the Vale where nobody can hear anybody talk about anybody. I sat there an hour and was happier than I have been since Naming Day.

Then one of the wolves opened its eyes and looked at me the way my aunt does, and I left.

title: A Pilgrim's Last Look
author: a pilgrim going south
body:
# For whoever sits here next

*A neat hand, a little shaky.*

---

I have sat here since noon looking at the green. They say take your last look and go. Nobody says how long a last look is allowed to be.

I can see Ashwell and the smoke from the well-house. I can see Hound Watch and the keeper on the crown, who waved. I waved back. That was a thing I did not expect: to be waved off.

I am going down to the line with a flask from the Wellspring to pour out, for my brother, who went in the Ash Winter's grandchildren's time and whose name the Order read. If you are coming back up: touch the stone and do not look round. If you are going down: look as long as you like. I did.

title: Behind the Turned Stone
author: the keeper of the Cliff Graves
body:
# For Tor, if he comes up

*Rookdown's grave-keeper, in pencil.*

---

It is Ide Rookwell's stone that has turned. Your great-aunt. I did not turn it. I have tried to turn it back and it will not go; it is set as if it was cut facing this way.

She drowned facing the Hush. Now she faces the village. I have thought about what the drowned would want to watch, if they were given the choice, and I think it is us.

I have left it. I have not told the bees. Somebody should.

title: The Boys' Floorstone Book
author: a Larkbourne Boy who could write
body:
# Floorstone

*In a carter's day-book. The carter's name on the cover has been scratched out with a knife.*

---

Six sacks to the man at the Flint Pits. He weighs them and does not ask. Two marks the sack.

Ten sacks. Jory says we should go further along the seam. Rab says not past the Fall. Rab is right.

Four sacks only. The knocking again. Ned put his ear to the Fall and says it is just the chalk settling. Ned is not the one who went to look.

Nine sacks. Somebody has been at our lanterns in the night and moved them all to the far end of the gallery, toward the Fall, in a row, lit.

The knapper woman came to the ladder head and called down to ask if we had heard them. We said no. She left a loaf on the ladder.

*Last, in a different hand:* Not past the Fall. Not for any money.

title: Seven and One
author: Abram Knapper, overman
body:
# On a prop at the Fall

*Written on the side of an oak pit-prop with a lump of chalk-stone, in capitals, the way a man writes in the dark.*

---

WE ARE SEVEN AND ME

AIR IS GOOD. WATER FROM THE SEAM.

HAL HURT. TOBY HURT. REST WELL.

WE HEAR YOU DIGGING. KNOCK AND WE WILL KNOCK.

*Lower down, smaller, in the same hand:*

NELL I HAVE THE TALLY. I WILL BRING THEM UP.

*Lower still, the strokes gone shaky:*

SEVEN AND ME

SEVEN AND ME

SEVEN AND

title: A Prospect of the Deep
author: three Knappers
body:
# A Prospect of the Deep

*A plan of the galleries in brown ink. The oldest notes are in a hand nobody writes any more.*

---

*In the oldest hand:* Here the floorstone, a man's height down from the wall-stone, the best in the down. Sink deep. The old pits did not go deep enough.

*In a second hand, beside a gallery drawn running east:* Seam breaks off over a hollow. Somebody has been here before us. Antler picks in the hollow, and they were not ours.

*In the third, Abram Knapper's, along the bottom:* Prop the night gallery before the thaw. The chalk is talking.

title: The Diggers' Map
author: the Wardens, and then the barrow-diggers
body:
# A survey of the Brow

*A Wardens' survey, the Roll's seal in the corner. Somebody has gone over it in red.*

---

Orm's Long Barrow. *(In red:)* DONE. Gold, two rings, a cup. Sold.

Tallow Barrow. *(In red:)* DONE. *(Crossed out. Under it:)* Walled up again. NOT BY US. Leave it.

The Lone Barrow. *(In red:)* nothing but a Warden. Left him.

The Hum Stone. *(In red, underlined twice:)* BRONZE. Four bands, a hand wide. And it HUMS now, Dunstan says, so there is more under it.

*In the margin, smaller, in another hand:* Dunstan, the dead come up the cliff to it. Ned saw them. Standing. Let it be.

title: A Rubbing off a Niche
author: a barrow-digger
body:
# Off a niche

*Charcoal rubbed on cloth. The Builders' letters, and under them a digger's guesses.*

---

VAEL · OROTH

*(Under it, in pencil:)* Same as on the Toll's crown, Ned says. Ned was a Sayer's boy once.

SUL · ANTHE · VAEL

*(Under it:)* Ned says this one means they were kept here. The ones in the niches. Kept, like you keep a note. Ned says they are still being kept, and that is what the humming is, and I said that is a lot of saying for a boy who left the Spire at twelve.

*(Lower:)* There's no gold in the niches. Only them.

title: A Digger's Last Reckoning
author: Dunstan Spade
body:
# Reckoning

*Pencil, on the back of a Tollmere broker's receipt for 'sundry grave-goods, old'.*

---

Bands off the stone: two. Sold one, Tollmere. Merrowby bellwright came out to the lip and shouted at us. Said every band we take a bell cracks in Merrowby. Ned laughed. I didn't.

The plate at the bottom. Biggest bronze I ever saw. Can't shift it. Rang it to find where it was hung and the dead stopped. All of them. Stood and listened till it died away.

They are between me and the lads now.

Rang it again. Again. They stand still as long as it rings. I can ring it a long time. I am the king of the barrows and I can ring a bell a long time.

*The last line has been gone over and over until the pencil went through.*

title: The Barrow-Wives' Rules
author: the barrow-wives of Wake Barrow
body:
# The Rules

*Scratched on a slate, both sides.*

---

Three nights for each. Not two. Two is how you get them back.

The lamp at the head, not the feet. They go toward it.

Tell them their name. Tell them they are dead. Tell them who is still alive. Tell them it is all right.

Do not eat in the barrow. Do not sleep in the barrow. Do not let them see you cry, they think it is for them and they stay.

Wash them in the spring first. They should go clean.

If there are too many, sit with them anyway.

*(Under it, newer, in another hand:)* If there are too many, sit with them anyway. — E.C.

title: A Warden's Report
author: Osric Hale, Warden of the Rest
body:
# Report, Wake Barrow

*On Rest paper. The ink has run where the crypt's damp got in.*

---

To the Roll room. As ordered, I went down Wake Barrow to see whether the Ash Winter's dead might be brought out and buried by the Rest and put on the Roll, so the Vale might stop keeping a lamp for them.

I went down past the hall with the benches and the pool. I came as far as these niches.

They are all here. More than the Roll has. I counted to four hundred and stopped.

There is a light below, very small. Somebody is talking down there, a woman, the same few words over and over, quite kindly.

I am leaving this here and going back up. I recommend that the Rest leave the lamp to the Crowles, and the barrow to whoever is talking.

*Osric Hale, Warden. The year after the Long Table was first laid.*

title: Ebba Crowle's Wake-Tally
author: Ebba Crowle, barrow-wife
body:
# The tally

*Birch-bark strips sewn together. Each strip a row of tallies, three strokes to a name, and the name beside them.*

---

Ald Merrow, three nights. Joan his wife, three nights. Their two, three nights, together, they were small.

Pell of Gosling Pit. Wat Cooper. Old Rook of Bramcombe, who would not lie down.

*(Strip after strip. The hand gets smaller, to fit more on.)*

I have done three hundred and twelve. The lamp oil is half. I will do them in twos now.

*(Later, smaller:)* In fours.

*(Later:)* The oil is out. I am doing it with the wick and the fat from the candles. I am telling them all at once now. It is not right. It is all I have.

*(The last strip, very small:)* Nobody has come down. That is good. That means they are eating up there.

I will tell myself last. Ebba Crowle. Three nights. When I have done the others.

title: A Letter from Harewell
author: nobody who gives a name
body:
*Birch-bark, a burnt stick, a round careful hand.*

---

Dear Mistress Cotter

Thank you for the letter. We read it out on the green. Everybody came.

We are all well. The well is well. Mother says to say the barley is in and it is a good barley, better than Larkstead's, and you are to tell Larkstead that.

We do not get many letters now. We used to get them from everywhere. Mother says it is because the roads have gone grey but I have been to the end of our road and it is only fog.

Please keep writing. When your letter comes the fog goes back a bit.

Your friend

*(The name has been written and rubbed out, and written and rubbed out, until there is a hole in the bark where it was.)*

title: Barred at Dawn
author: Aldous Pomfrey, press-master of the Great Press
body:
*A slate, scratched with a nail.*

---

Twelfth Night. The King crowned, Hob Applegarth, a good King, loud, kind to the young ones. The trees beaten and toasted. All down to the Vat at midnight to wake her.

Dawn. I called the crown up. The King would not give it. He said the singing was too good to stop, and that he would stop it when it was finished, and that it was not finished. The wassailers would not come up without him.

I have called three times as the rules say. I have barred the door as the rules say. A King who will not give back the crown keeps the cellar, and the cellar keeps him.

God keep the orchard. I do not think anybody will press here again.

*(Under it, newer, in a different hand:)* Forty years. Still singing. -- P.A.

title: The Wassail Roll
author: the press-masters of Wassail Knap
body:
# The Kings

*Each King's name, the year, and the hour the crown came back up the stair.*

---

Old Pell Hazel, cock-crow.
Wat Cider, first light.
Meg Pomfrey, the first Queen, an hour before dawn, and she said it was too early.
Ald Tamwick, cock-crow, and drunk.
*(Dozens more, the hours all early, the hands all different.)*

---

Hob Applegarth.

*There is no hour beside his name. Someone has written one in later, very small, and crossed it out:* when it is finished.

title: The Pickers' Tally
author: the Hazelcombe pickers
body:
*A hazel stick, notched.*

---

EDDY. JOAN. LITTLE NAT.

Twenty-two bushel, the notches say, off trees that have not borne in forty years, picked at night by lantern, in blossom and fruit at once.

The last notch is cut deeper than the others, as if whoever cut it was being hurried, or was dancing.

title: A Letter to Gosford
author: Wenna Cotter, cote-wife
body:
*Birch-bark, soot-ink, a quick round hand; red thread, untied.*

---

To Gosford, the green, whoever reads it out.

News this week. Rookdown's bees have swarmed into the Moot and the rooks are furious. Ashwell's well is sweet again. The Knap has blossomed, all of it, at midnight, and Pip Applegarth is sitting up there in a hut like her gran used to. Tamwick has a cow with two calves. Merrowby is Merrowby.

You are not forgotten. I said your name to a carter this morning and he said it back.

Write if you can. Larkstead does now. Harewell does.

W.C.

*(On the back, in the same hand, later:)* The bird won't go. Third week. It sits on the lantern and looks west and won't go. -- Keeping it for next week.

title: The Troy Book
author: Maudie Twelvetrees, keeper of Tamwick Troy
body:
# Names said at the heart

*A ribbon pressed between every page. A name a line, and who walked them in.*

---

Ald Twelvetrees. Rosie Cider. Hob Applegarth, who ran it and had to go round again.

Pip Applegarth, who would not cry. Nat Hazel, who did.

*(Fifty years of Naming Days. Lately, at the bottom of each page, grown hands:)*

My own name, Joan Cooper of Merrowby, aged sixty, because I could not think of it on Tuesday.

My husband's, because I am afraid I will lose his before I lose mine.

---

*The last line, in Maudie's hand:* A ribbon tied this morning with no name on it and nobody walked in. I have walked it three times myself to see who is at the heart. Nobody. -- M.T.

title: The Court of Rooks
author: the rook-wives of the Witness Elms
body:
# The rook-wife's oath

*Scratched on a slate under the elms, each year's added below.*

---

I have told what the rooks showed me and no more and no less. I have taken bright things and given what was seen. I have not killed a rook nor let one be killed. If I lie the rooks may have my eyes, which they have always wanted.

---

*This year's witness, in Hester Corvey's hand:*

The rooks have seen: the Larkbourne Boys on the Ford road, nine of them. A light in the Briar. A man in a grey coat in the Scarecrow Moot who did not move for a summer. A dove going into the fog on the West Downs and coming back.

They have begun leaving bright things on the stump for me. A brass button off a Warden's coat. A child's ring. A bell-clapper. I do not know what they want shown.

title: The Last Tally
author: Wat Southgate, tithe-reeve
body:
*An ash tally, notched, the halves bound with wire.*

---

Three hundred and twelve stooks off the East Downs. In. The Briar carts to come Michaelmas.

The kern-baby plaited from Southgate's last sheaf by my wife, crowned, and hung on the tie-beam as is right. To come down Plough Monday and go into the first furrow.

*(Burnt in at the end, deep:)* The Briar is shut. No carts. We cannot sell it and cannot eat it all and the roof is going. The men are to have their supper in the loft and sleep there the night as they always do.

*There is no mark for Plough Monday.*

title: Harvest Supper
author: the Southgate reaping gang
body:
*Chalk on slate, a gang's names in a ring, the way they sat.*

---

Wat at the head. Long Tom. Jem and his brother. The Hesta girl with the cider. Old Pell who has cut the last sheaf forty years.

Round the ring, under every name, a mark for every jug.

*At the bottom, in a hand that has had a good many jugs:* we will carry her out Plough Monday, the Mother, and sing her into the furrow, and then we will all go home. -- Pell.
